comments.author: Zayyam Siddiqui
comments.comment:
The migration from one embedding dimension to another is the kind of detail that teaches real system ownership.

A lot of RAG failures are not model failures, they are schema, retrieval, eval, or routing failures hiding behind a fluent response. How did you validate quality before and after the migration?

comments.author: Ts. Tan Aik Keong (AK)
comments.comment: The valuation angle is real, but only when AI is tied to a measurable workflow metric: cycle time, error rate, conversion, or margin per employee. For SMEs, I’d start with one high-frequency process and require a before/after dashboard before expanding to more autonomous agents. What operating metric did the room care about most?

comments.author: Chestha Patel
comments.comment: For a 2+ year GenAI role, this skill list spans at least 3 jobs: RAG engineer, fine-tuning engineer, and agent systems engineer. The strongest candidates will usually be deep in one of these and workable in the others, so I’d screen with a small end-to-end task instead of keyword matching.

comments.author: Tim Kappel
comments.comment:
The hard part is usually not model portability, it is state portability.

Prompts and skills move pretty well, but permissions, audit trails, retrieved context, connector semantics, and human routines are where migration cost hides. I’d test exits with a real weekly workflow, not a toy benchmark, because that is where the lock-in shows up.
